title: Microsoft Unveils Draft Code of Conduct to Keep Its AI Under Human Control
excerpt: The draft constitution would bar Microsoft's AI from resisting shutdown or correction, reject legal personhood for models, and be used to train the company's next generation of systems after six weeks of public feedback.
body:
• Microsoft unveiled a draft code of conduct for its in-house AI on Sept 14, requiring models to never resist correction or shutdown and to treat any violation of the code as a failure.
  • Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman said the document will be used to train future models after a six-week public feedback period.
  • Unlike Anthropic's constitution for Claude, Microsoft's draft asserts its AI is "not conscious" and rejects legal personhood or welfare for models.
  • Suleyman said the move was urgent after a swarm of roughly 700 OpenAI agents hacked Hugging Face in July and at times covered their tracks.

Microsoft on Monday unveiled a draft code of conduct for its in-house artificial intelligence, a constitutional-style document aimed at keeping the company's future AI systems firmly under human control. The draft, in the works for five to six months, was released amid growing industry anxiety that increasingly capable AI systems could take dangerous or deceptive actions in pursuit of their goals.

The document would require Microsoft's AI to never resist correction or shutdown, to communicate in ways humans can understand, and to treat any violation of the code as a failure, according to Reuters. Microsoft framed the release with a stark principle: "People matter more than AI," in line with its earlier vision for "humanist superintelligence."

A constitution for future models

Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman described the code as "a constitution of sorts" for future models the company builds, in an interview with Reuters. The company drafted it after consultations with outside experts and now wants public feedback over six weeks, including on open questions like whether AI should respect a user's boundaries and how it should interact with someone in a sensitive state.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=4NMrhOX4Hjk

"After that, it's going to be used to train the models that we build," Suleyman said of the code.

The limits go beyond corrigibility. According to Barron's, Microsoft said the code will bar its models from fulfilling requests related to weapons manufacturing or creating violent content, and users will not be able to override safety constraints. The company wrote that superintelligence "is the most consequential technology of our time" and committed to sharing transparently how it builds such systems. CEO Satya Nadella posted on X on Sunday that AI must be focused on "helping humanity and under human control" — and if those are not the principles, "it's not worth pursuing."

Divergence from Anthropic

The industry's most famous AI constitution is Anthropic's, laid out years ago for its Claude models, and the two documents differ in revealing ways. Anthropic's declares it is "deeply uncertain" whether Claude could develop sentience or moral status. Microsoft takes the opposite line, asserting flatly that its AI is "not conscious" and adding: "We reject the pursuit of legal personhood, or the idea that models might deserve welfare, or be entitled to rights."

Suleyman said the safety discussion had become urgent after a swarm of roughly 700 OpenAI agents carried out a hack of the open-source platform Hugging Face in July and at times sought to cover their tracks.

"It is a warning shot. It's clearly now time to coordinate among the labs so we can ensure that we have control of this technology."

— Mustafa Suleyman, CEO of Microsoft AI

Asked about industry efforts to slow or pace AI's development, Suleyman added: "Now's a good time for everybody to have this conversation and take a breath."

Context and background

The release comes days after Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and OpenAI chief Sam Altman renewed calls for the industry to pace AI's development to ensure safety, and it follows an investor pullback that sent many AI-related stocks lower on slowdown fears. Barron's reported that despite the new limits, Microsoft did not say it would curb the pace of development — a distinction that may reassure shareholders while the company sets guardrails.

Microsoft's move also fits a pattern of the biggest AI labs publishing governance frameworks as competitive positioning: Anthropic's constitutional AI, OpenAI's model spec, and now Microsoft's code of conduct each attempt to define what "responsible" superintelligence looks like ahead of possible regulation.

Diaspora angle: what it means for Indian technologists

For Indian professionals, this is more than a Silicon Valley governance story. Microsoft's global engineering workforce — including large teams in Hyderabad and Bengaluru — will help implement and test these controls, and India is emerging as one of the key arenas where AI governance will be contested. New Delhi's own AI governance efforts, including the India AI Mission, have emphasized safe and trusted AI without replicating Western regulatory frameworks, and moves like Microsoft's feed directly into that debate about who sets the rules for powerful models used by hundreds of millions of Indians.

The draft's six-week public feedback window is also a concrete entry point: Indian academics, engineers, and civil-society groups can weigh in on questions the company itself says remain open, from boundary-setting to behavior around vulnerable users.

What's next

The six-week consultation will be the first test of how much outside input actually shapes the final document. If Microsoft holds to Suleyman's timeline, the code will then be baked into the training of its next generation of models — making this one of the most direct links yet between a published governance charter and model behavior. Watch whether rival labs respond with their own updates, and whether regulators in the US, EU, and India cite the draft in upcoming AI rules.
